title: "Checking the Proportional Hazards Assumption"
execute:
  echo: false
format: html
---

```{r}
#| warning: false
library(survival)
library(survminer)
```

## Learning Objectives

- Interpret a complementary log-log plot
- Interpret Schoenfeld residual tests
- Interpret Schoenfeld residual plots


## Lesson

Proportional hazards is a strong assumption.
So, we really should check it before interpreting the results
of a Cox regression model.
How do we check this assumption?
I'm going to present two methods.

### Complementary Log-Log Plot

Recall that proportional hazards means $h_2(t) = ch_1(t)$,
where $h_2(t)$ denotes the hazard rate at time $t$ for group 2,
$h_1(t)$ denotes the hazard rate at time $t$ for group 1,
and $c$ is a positive constant.
Proportional hazards implies
$$
\begin{align*}
h_2(t) &= ch_1(t) \\
\int_0^t h_2(s)\,ds &= \int_0^t ch_1(s) \,ds \\
\int_0^t h_2(s)\,ds &= c \int_0^t h_1(s) \,ds \\
\Lambda_2(t) &= c\Lambda_1(t) \\
-\log S_2(t) &= -c\log S_1(t) \\
\log(-\log S_2(t)) &= \log(-c\log S_1(t)) \\
\log(-\log S_2(t)) &= \log c + \log(-\log S_1(t)) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
$$
How is this helpful to us?
Well, we know how to estimate $S_2(t)$ and $S_1(t)$:
we can create Kaplan-Meier curves.
If we plot $\log(-\log \hat{S}_2(t))$ and $\log(-\log \hat{S}_1(t))$,
and the two curves are parallel,
that's evidence for proportional hazards.


```{r}
d_colon <- colon

# Just death, not recurrence
d_colon <- d_colon[d_colon$etype == 2, ]
```

Let's look at an example.
Let's return to the data from the trial comparing two adjuvant therapy regimens
for colon cancer
([Moertel et al., 1995](https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-122-5-199503010-00001)).
These are the variables:

- `time`: Time until death in days. Unfortunately, I don't know the time origin.
- `status`: 1 is death, 0 is censoring.
- `rx`: This is the treatment variable, and it has three levels:
`Obs` for observation; `Lev` for Levamisole,
and `Lev+5FU` for Levamisole plus 5-FU.
- `sex`: 1 for male, 0 for female.
- `age`: This is in years, but I don't know when it was measured.
Maybe at the time origin?

We can look at a complementary log-log plot to check for proportional hazards
by treatment.

```{r}
#| echo: true
# Complementary log-log plot
ggsurvplot(fit = survfit(Surv(time = time,
                              event = status) ~ rx,
                         data = d_colon),
           fun = "cloglog")
```

These lines are clearly not parallel. They intersect multiple times.

What if we stratify by sex?

```{r}
#| echo: true
# Complementary log-log plot
ggsurvplot(fit = survfit(Surv(time = time,
                              event = status) ~ sex,
                         data = d_colon),
           fun = "cloglog")
```
These are also not parallel.

So far, we don't have evidence for proportional hazards in our data.
However it's worth noting that the complementary log-log plot
requires splitting the data set into groups.
If we tried to make such a plot for a model
with treatment, sex, and age as explanatory variables,
it would include a separate curve for each unique combination of treatment,
sex and age.
That's not really feasible for a model with many variables,
or a model with even a few continuous variables.

### Schoenfeld Residuals

Schoenfeld residuals are another way to assess the proportional hazards
assumption for a given model.
Fortunately, they can be used even when there are many covariates in the
model,
and/or continuous covariates.
I'm not going to get into how Schoenfeld residuals are computed,
but I'll explain how to intepret the associated hypothesis tests
and plots.

If you use the function `cox.zph` from the package `survival`,
it will perform a few hypothesis tests:
one for each explanatory variable in the model, and another global test.
The null hypothesis for a specific covariate is that the proportional
hazards assumption holds for that covariate.
The null hypothesis for the global test is that the proportional hazards
assumption holds for the model as a whole.

```{r}
#| echo: true
# Cox regression
mod_01 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = time,
                               event = status) ~ rx + sex + age,
                data = d_colon)

# Schoenfeld residual test
mod_01_ph_test <- cox.zph(mod_01)
mod_01_ph_test
```

We can see above that the p-values for every test are higher than any
reasonable cutoff.
This means that we fail to reject the hypotheses that the proportional hazards
assumption holds for treatment, sex, age, and the model as a whole.
This means we can interpret our coefficients.

Note that this contradicts what we saw in the complementary log-log plots.
I would trust the Schoenfeld residuals test more than the complementary log-log
plots for this example because we weren't able to make a single
complementary log-log plot that accounted for every covariate in the model.

What if we rejected the null for some covariates but not others,
or for the global test but not the covariate-specific tests?
I would recommend looking at the Schoenfeld residual plots to get a better
sense of what's going on.
Actually, I would look at the Schoenfeld residual plots no matter what
the tests say.


```{r}
#| echo: true
# Plots
plot(mod_01_ph_test)
ggcoxzph(mod_01_ph_test)
```

In the code above, I've used both base R plotting and the function
`ggcoxzph` from the package `survminer`.
You only need to do one or the other.

In each plot, time is on the horizontal axis and `Beta(t)` for a specific
covariate is on the vertical axis.
These plots are trying to display graphically how the estimated coefficient
changes over time.
The proportional hazards assumption means that the coefficient doesn't
change over time.
So, if the curve is flat,
that's evidence for the proportional hazards assumption being correct.
In all the plots above,
the curve is flat, which is consistent with the results from the Schoenfeld
residuals test.

If you find, through either the test or the plots,
that the proportional hazards assumption doesn't hold,
you may have to use other methods and/or change your model.

## Problems

### Problem 1

Let's return to the diabetic retinopathy data set.
As a reminder, each row corresponds to the left eye of a patient
with "high-risk" diabetic retinopathy.
The explanatory variables are as follows:

- `age`: Age at diagnosis.
- `trt`: Treatment (0 = no treatment, 1 = laser).
- `risk_factor`: Risk group, with values 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12.
I'm not sure why there's no 7.

```{r}
d_dr <- diabetic
d_dr <- d_dr[d_dr$eye == "left", ]
d_dr$risk_factor <- as.factor(d_dr$risk)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
mod_02 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = time,
                               event = status) ~ age + trt + risk_factor,
                data = d_dr)
mod_02_ph_test <- cox.zph(mod_02)
ggcoxzph(mod_02_ph_test)
```

Is the proportional hazards assumption met for this model?
Justify your answer.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

All the p-values for the hypothesis tests are large,
and the curves in the plots are flat,
indicating the proportional hazards assumption is met for this model.

:::
